body:
From individual reformers to collective organizations

By the late 19th and early 20th centuries, women were increasingly participating directly in organized social reform. They founded associations, established schools, published their views and demanded legal and political changes.

This development was significant because women were no longer represented only as beneficiaries of reforms proposed by others. They increasingly became leaders and organizers of campaigns for their own rights.

Important women's organizations

Arya Mahila Samaj, 1882

Pandita Ramabai established the Arya Mahila Samaj in 1882 in Pune. It sought to improve the position of women, particularly through education and social reform.

Bharat Stree Mahamandal, 1910

Sarala Devi Chaudhurani founded the Bharat Stree Mahamandal in 1910 at Allahabad. The organization promoted women's education and collective advancement.

Women's Indian Association, 1917

The Women's Indian Association (WIA) was formed in 1917 at Adyar, Madras, now part of Chennai. Major figures associated with its establishment included Annie Besant, Margaret Cousins and Dorothy Jinarajadasa.

The association supported girls' education, opposition to child marriage and women's participation in public affairs. It also campaigned for women's suffrage, meaning the right of women to vote.

All India Women's Conference, 1927

The All India Women's Conference (AIWC) was established in 1927, with Margaret Cousins playing a leading role in its formation and organization.

Its first conference was held at Pune. Education was an important initial concern, and the organization subsequently became active in campaigns concerning marriage laws, women's status and social welfare.

Gujarat connection: Maharani Chimnabai Gaekwad

The first president of the All India Women's Conference in 1927 was Maharani Chimnabai Gaekwad of Baroda.

She was associated with efforts to advance women's education and improve women's position in society. Her participation connected the early national women's movement with reform initiatives in Baroda, in present-day Gujarat.

Another figure associated with Gujarat, Vidyagauri Nilkanth, served as AIWC president in 1933.

AIWC, 1927: Margaret Cousins played a leading founding role; the first conference took place in Pune; Maharani Chimnabai Gaekwad of Baroda was the first president.

Connecting the major reform milestones

The major anti-caste milestones can be followed through 1873, when Phule founded Satyashodhak Samaj; 1888, when Narayana Guru performed the Aruvippuram consecration; 1903, when SNDP Yogam was founded; 1925, when Periyar launched the Self-Respect Movement; 1927, when Ambedkar led the Mahad Satyagraha; and 1932, when the Poona Pact addressed political representation.

Major milestones in women's social and legal reform include 1829, the prohibition of sati under the Bengal regulation; 1848, the opening of the Phules' school for girls at Pune; 1856, Hindu widow remarriage legislation; 1891, the Age of Consent Act; 1929, the Child Marriage Restraint Act; 1937, improved property rights for certain Hindu widows; 1956, the Hindu Succession Act; and 2005, the amendment strengthening daughters' coparcenary rights.

These developments should be understood as related but distinct efforts. Some challenged discriminatory customs directly. Others established educational opportunities, created associations, protected civil rights or changed the law.

How to distinguish closely related facts

  • Phule and Pandita Ramabai: Both supported women's advancement, but Phule founded Satyashodhak Samaj and Ramabai founded Arya Mahila Samaj.
  • WIA and AIWC: Women's Indian Association began in 1917; All India Women's Conference began in 1927.
  • Mahad and Kalaram: Mahad concerned a public water tank in 1927; Kalaram concerned temple entry in 1930.
  • Age of consent and age of marriage: The 1891 and 1929 laws addressed different legal questions.
  • Property ownership and coparcenary: Section 14 of the 1956 Hindu Succession Act and the 2005 amendment to section 6 addressed different rights.

Prelims focus

  • 1882: Pandita Ramabai founded Arya Mahila Samaj.
  • 1910: Sarala Devi Chaudhurani founded Bharat Stree Mahamandal.
  • 1917: Women's Indian Association established at Adyar, Madras.
  • 1927: All India Women's Conference established; first conference in Pune.
  • 1927: Maharani Chimnabai Gaekwad of Baroda was AIWC's first president.
  • Trap: Margaret Cousins was a major founder and organizer of AIWC, but its first president was Maharani Chimnabai Gaekwad.
